draft.title: Language and identity
card: The words we choose show who we are. They can hint at where we live, how old we are and which groups we belong to. Sharing a group's words can help people feel they belong.
Slang
informal words used mostly among friends or people of a similar age, such as "sick" to mean great.
Local saying
a word or phrase used mainly in one place or region, such as "port" for a school bag, which many people say in Victoria.
Idiom
a phrase whose meaning is not the same as its separate words, such as "under the weather" for feeling unwell.
draft.remember: The words we share with others can mark our age, our place and our groups.

a.q: After landing a new trick, Jai says it was "mad", meaning it was excellent. What kind of language is this?
opts: Slang, informal words used among friends
An idiom, a fixed phrase with a hidden meaning
A local saying, used mainly in one region
Formal language, suited to a school essay
a.why: Using "mad" to mean excellent gives an everyday word a new, informal meaning, like "sick" for great, so it is slang. It is not an idiom, because an idiom is a phrase whose meaning differs from its separate words, and "mad" is a single word.
a.clue: Is this one word with a new meaning, or a whole phrase?

b.q: Priya moves from Geelong to a new school in Mildura. Within a few weeks she is saying the same phrases as her new classmates. What does this most likely show?
opts: She is taking on shared words to fit in
Her word choices have no link to her identity
She can no longer speak in a formal way
She wants to sound more formal at school
b.why: People often take on the words of a group to show they belong, so Priya's new phrases help her fit in. It does not mean she cannot speak formally, because speakers can change their words to suit who they are talking to.
b.clue: Why might someone start talking like a new group?

proposal.title: Language and identity
card: Our words, accent and how formal we sound can show our age, where we live and which groups we belong to. Sharing a group's words can help people feel they belong.
Slang
informal words used mostly among friends or people of a similar age, such as "sick" to mean great.
Local saying
a word or phrase used mainly in one place, such as "potato cake" in Victoria for the fried potato slice called a scallop in NSW.
Idiom
a phrase whose meaning is not the same as its separate words, such as "under the weather" for feeling unwell.
proposal.remember: Language works like a badge: the words we share mark the groups we belong to.
